question: Which combination of anaesthetic techniques most effectively reduces the risk of postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) in a high-risk day-surgery patient?

answers.text: Volatile induction and maintenance with sevoflurane + opioid analgesia + routine antiemetic at end of surgery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Volatile agents and opioids are both independent risk factors for PONV; this strategy is the opposite of best practice in high-risk patients.

answers.text: TIVA with propofol + regional analgesia (avoiding opioids) + two prophylactic antiemetics (multimodal)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The Apfel risk-reduction strategy for high-risk PONV patients combines: propofol TIVA (intrinsic anti-emetic), opioid-sparing analgesia (regional/NSAIDs), and multimodal antiemetics (e.g., ondansetron + dexamethasone).

answers.text: Propofol induction then isoflurane maintenance + dexamethasone 8mg IV

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Switching to a volatile agent for maintenance reintroduces a major PONV trigger; a single antiemetic alone is insufficient for high-risk patients.

answers.text: Ketamine infusion + high-dose opioids to reduce volatile agent requirement

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ketamine can contribute to postoperative nausea; high-dose opioids are a strong independent PONV risk factor — this approach worsens risk.

overallFeedback.feedback: For high-risk PONV: use propofol TIVA (not volatile agents), minimise opioids with regional/NSAID analgesia, and give at least two prophylactic antiemetics from different classes.
Excellent. PONV prophylaxis in high-risk patients requires a multimodal strategy: TIVA (propofol), opioid-sparing analgesia, and combination antiemetics (at least two agents from different classes).
